feedback: If a learner gives 3 for 3.7: on the number line show that 3.7 is only 0.3 away from 4 but 0.7 away from 3, so it is nearer 4; contrast this with simply chopping off the part after the point.
If a learner gives 4 for 3.2: mark the halfway point 3.5 and show 3.2 sits below it, in the lower half, so it is nearer 3 — having 'something after the point' does not automatically mean round up.
If a learner is unsure what rounding means: contrast rounding 3.7 (to 4, the nearer whole) with chopping/truncating 3.7 (to 3, just dropping the part after the point) so the difference is explicit.
Reinforce correct reasoning by asking the learner to justify each answer by distance rather than by reciting a rule.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding is a nearness judgement on a line: the whole you round to is the one the number is closer to. The tenths digit is a shortcut that reports which half of the interval you are in, not an arbitrary 'chop or bump' instruction.
learnerActions: Draw or use a number line from 3 to 4 with each tenth marked, and plot 3.7 on it.
Ask aloud: is 3.7 nearer to 3 or to 4, and roughly how much nearer? Measure or count the gaps (0.3 to 4, 0.7 to 3).
Plot 3.2 on the same line and decide which whole it is nearer, explaining from the position (0.2 to 3, 0.8 to 4).
Mark the halfway point 3.5 and say what is special about it.
Repeat with a fresh set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 2.8, 5.1, 7.4), stating each result and why.

Finally state the rule in your own words as a consequence of distance: 'look at the tenths — if it is in the lower half it rounds down, in the upper half it rounds up, and the exact midpoint follows the agreed convention.'
activities.title: Which whole is it nearest? Placing decimals on a number line

feedback: If a learner gives 6 for 6.5 or hesitates: establish first that 6.5 is equidistant from 6 and 7, then introduce 'round half up' as a shared rule everyone agrees to use.
If a learner thinks the midpoint 'obviously' goes up for a distance reason: clarify that both wholes are exactly as far away, so the up-choice is a convention, not because 7 is nearer.
Praise a learner who can say 6.5 is the special equidistant case and that the convention is a choice.
activities.intendedInsight: The exact midpoint is the one case nearness does not settle because it is equidistant; 'round half up' is an agreed convention introduced once 'nearest' is secure, not an extension of the distance rule.
learnerActions: On a number line from 6 to 7, place 6.5 and measure its distance to 6 and to 7.
Confirm that 6.5 is exactly halfway — equally far from both wholes — so distance alone cannot decide.
Discuss who decides what happens here, and learn that the agreed convention is 'round half up', so 6.5 rounds to 7.
Try other midpoints (e.g. 2.5, 4.5) and apply the same agreed convention, stating that this is a shared choice, not a distance fact.
Explain in your own words the difference between 6.5 (needs the convention) and 6.7 (decided by nearness).
activities.title: The midpoint x.5 and the round-up convention

feedback: If a learner sorts 3.5 into 'rounds to 3': remind them it is the equidistant midpoint and the agreed convention sends it up to 4.
If a learner sorts 3.2 into 'rounds to 4': return to the halfway mark and show 3.2 is in the lower half, nearer 3.
If a learner sorts everything with a decimal into 'rounds to 4': this is the always-up error — check each against the midpoint.
Confirm a correct sort by asking the learner to re-state the rule as a consequence of nearness.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding a set is cleanly checkable, and articulating why each number rounds as it does consolidates the distance-based reason behind the digit rule.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of one-decimal-place numbers (e.g. 3.1, 3.7, 3.5, 3.4, 3.8, 3.2) and sort each into 'rounds to 3' or 'rounds to 4'.
For each number, say its distance to each whole, or which half it is in, to justify your sort.

Round 3.7 correctly to 4, then show the two common error patterns on the numbers where each actually goes wrong: truncation wrongly gives 3 for 3.7 (dropping the part after the point), while the always-up error wrongly sends numbers like 3.2 to 4.
Check your whole set by estimating and asking whether each answer is sensible.
State the rounding rule aloud as a summary of what the sort shows.
activities.title: Sort and check a set of roundings
